pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, sorting into categories is the first act of the whole statistical process (GAISE Level A): choose an attribute, classify every object by it into non-overlapping groups, count each group, and order the groups by count to see which has most/fewest. The teaching job is to make the sorting RULE explicit and consistent (one attribute at a time), to physically arrange the sorted groups so counts can be compared, and to connect the activity to a real question ('which colour do we have most of?'). Best done with real objects the child handles — lining up or bins — so the counts are concrete before any chart appears.
bestPractices: Name the single sorting attribute out loud before sorting ('we are sorting by COLOUR') and keep it fixed, so groups don't drift into mixed criteria
Arrange sorted groups as equal-spaced lines or stacks (a proto-bar-graph) so 'most/fewest' can be read by comparing counts, not the space objects happen to fill
Sort the SAME set two different ways (by colour, then by size) so the child sees the data is fixed but the grouping is a choice
Anchor to a real question and read the result back ('so we have most red — does that answer our question?') to build early data sense
keyRepresentations: Sorting hoops / bins or trays, one per category
Objects lined up one-to-one in rows (an emerging bar graph)
A simple two- or three-row count record (category name + count)
Real class data the child helped generate (favourite colour, shape cards)
commonMisconceptions: Shifts the sorting criterion partway (starts by colour, drifts to size), producing mixed groups
Judges 'most' by the space a group takes up rather than its count (a spread-out group of big objects looks like 'more')
Miscounts a group by losing track when objects are scattered (insecure cardinality)
Thinks each object can go in more than one pile, or leaves objects unsorted

learn.summary: For 5-6 year olds, sorting into categories is an early step of the statistical process, after posing a question: choose one attribute, classify every object into non-overlapping groups, count each group, and order groups by count to find most/fewest. Make the sorting RULE explicit and fixed (one attribute at a time), physically arrange groups so counts can be compared fairly, and anchor to a real question ('which colour do we have most of?'). Work with real objects the child handles so counts are concrete before any chart appears.

activities.title: Drag-to-sort (or hands-on sort) with self-counting groups
feedback: If groups end up containing more than one colour, name the one attribute aloud again ('everything by COLOUR'), hold up a shape and ask 'what colour — so which group?', and re-sort together.

If the child names the group that fills more space as 'most', line both groups up one-to-one (one object opposite one object) and count: show that the group that spread over more space can actually have fewer — the group with objects left unmatched has more.

If the count of a scattered group is unstable, slide or set each object aside as it is counted, or line the group up first, so the last number said is how many; this is a counting lapse to steady, not a sorting error.
When re-sorting by size changes the counts, ask 'same shapes — why are the piles different now?' to surface that grouping is a choice.
activities.rationale: At GAISE Level A, sorting and counting are early steps of the statistical process (after posing a question): children represent how many times each outcome occurs and identify the most frequent. Direct handling lets the child act, see each category total grow, and read most/fewest from counts rather than appearance. An optional self-counting on-screen mat (bins with live counters rendered as stacks of equal-sized units, plus a 're-sort by size' button) can make the count-and-compare mechanism visible; physical lines with one object per equal-sized space, or stacks of same-size counters, achieve the same comparison with real objects.
sourceClaims: Sorting is the entry point of statistics: at Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable (how many times each outcome occurs) using tables and picture/bar graphs, e.g. young children line up by favourite music type and count each category; the mode is the most frequent outcome

Year 2 pupils are taught to ask and answer questions by counting the number of objects in each category and sorting the categories by quantity, and to ask and answer questions about totalling and comparing categorical data
learnerActions: Face a jumble of coloured shapes and three labelled groups/bins (physical trays or an on-screen mat).
Before starting, say aloud the single attribute: 'we are sorting by COLOUR.'
Move each shape into its matching group until every shape is placed and none is left over.

Watch or build each group as a line with one object per equal-sized space (or a stack of same-size counters standing for the objects) so groups can be compared fairly, and keep a running count of each group.
Read off which group has the most and which has the fewest by comparing the counts.
Then re-sort the SAME set a different way (by size): tip everything out, relabel the groups, and sort again, noticing the counts change.
activities.intendedInsight: Sorting means applying one consistent rule to classify every object, and 'most/fewest' is read from the counts once the groups are arranged for fair comparison. The same fixed data can also be grouped in more than one way — how you sort is a choice.

activities.title: Sort the same set two different ways
feedback: If the child treats the second sort as a 'wrong answer' to the first, remind them both sorts are correct — they just answer different questions.
If criteria drift mid-sort, pause and restate the single attribute for that round before continuing.
activities.rationale: Sorting the same set by two attributes separates the stable data from the chosen grouping rule, building early data sense and reinforcing that a single attribute must be held fixed within one sort.
learnerActions: Take one set of objects and sort it by colour; count and record each group (category name + count).
Tip the set out and sort the SAME objects by a second attribute (size: big/small); count and record again.
Compare the two records and talk about how the groups and their counts differ even though the objects are identical.
activities.intendedInsight: The data is fixed, but the grouping is a choice; different attributes give different groups and different counts.

activities.title: Answer a real question from sorted class data
feedback: If the child reports a group without tying it back to the question, re-ask the original question and have them connect the count to it.
Ask 'how do you know that group has the most — can you show me?' to check the answer rests on counting, not appearance.
activities.rationale: Anchoring to a genuine question and reading the result back builds early data sense and completes the statistical cycle from question to conclusion.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils are taught to ask and answer questions by counting the number of objects in each category and sorting the categories by quantity, and to ask and answer questions about totalling and comparing categorical data
learnerActions: Pose a real question first, e.g. 'which colour do we have most of?' or use data the child helped generate (favourite colour, shape cards).
Sort and count to answer it, then read the result back against the question: 'so we have most red — does that answer our question?'
State both the most and the fewest category by their counts (or say that groups tie when their counts are equal).
activities.intendedInsight: Sorting and counting are done for a purpose — to answer a question about real data — not as an isolated exercise.

constraints: Keep one sorting attribute fixed within a single sort; name it aloud before starting so groups don't drift into mixed criteria.

Arrange groups as lines with one object per equal-sized space (e.g. a grid mat), or as stacks of same-size counters or blocks, so 'most/fewest' is read from count, not from the space a group happens to fill — large or spread-out objects can look like 'more' while being fewer, and stacks of different-sized shapes cannot be fairly compared by height.
Every object must be classified into exactly one non-overlapping group; none left unsorted and none in two piles.
Secure cardinality supports this skill: if a child loses track counting a scattered group, that is a counting lapse to steady (slide each aside / line them up), not a sorting error to reteach.

Assess by watching the child sort and count (the doing), not by asking them to describe sorting: observe whether they hold one rule, sort exhaustively, count with cardinality, and read most/fewest from counts. Recognising an answer in a multiple-choice check is not the same as independently sorting and counting.
A tap-to-reveal of an already-sorted set with counts can serve as reference, but it does not let the child perform the sorting, which is the skill; use it only as a scaffold, not the main task.

An open conversation or a 3D handling task is not required for this flat, single-attribute classification; a multiple-choice 'which has most?' may check the read-off, but recognising the answer does not elicit independent sorting and counting.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated a self-counting 2D drag-to-sort mat as 'ideal' and claimed a quiz 'cannot let the child DO the sorting' and that '3D adds handling load without insight'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy claims; retained as narrowly scoped affordance/limit notes (self-counting bins make the mechanism visible; recognition-only responses don't elicit independent construction) rather than universal laws. Physical objects achieve the same learning and the source itself recommends real objects.

Activity 2 (re-sort the same set) and the 'grouping is a choice' element of activity 1's insight are best practice from the pedagogy text but are not directly supported by either source claim; activity 2's sourceClaims is therefore []. Activity 1's cited claims support its core sorting/counting/most-fewest principle, not the re-sort-is-a-choice extension. The National Curriculum 'ask and answer questions' claim is the direct support for the real-question activity.

Self-audit: the most/fewest-by-space misconception and its fix (line up one-to-one and count) are internally consistent; the re-sort-changes-counts point correctly keeps the data fixed while the grouping varies. No arithmetic, force/motion, fraction, or shade content to check. The reteachPrerequisiteId for the space-vs-count error is retained as a signal in the original row but omitted from learner-facing text as an internal catalog reference.

probeDeeper: Ask 'how did you decide where this one goes?' to check the sorting rule is conscious and consistent
Counterexample tuned to this age: hand them a counter that could fit two ideas (a big red one while sorting by colour) and watch whether they hold the colour rule
Ask 'how do you know that pile has the most — can you show me?' to see whether 'most' rests on counting or on appearance
Ask 'could we sort these a different way?' to check they grasp that grouping is a choice, not fixed
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: the child picks one attribute (colour) and sorts EVERY counter into non-overlapping groups, counts each group accurately (last-number-said = how many), and names the largest and smallest groups by their counts — ideally lining the groups up to compare.

errorPatterns.pattern: Shifts the sorting criterion partway — begins by colour then starts grouping by size or shape, ending with mixed piles
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the one attribute aloud ('everything sorted by COLOUR') and re-sort together; hold up a counter and ask 'what colour — so which pile?' to fix the single rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The finished groups contain more than one colour, or the child hesitates over where a big red counter goes

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges 'most' by the space a group occupies rather than its count — a spread-out or larger-object group looks like more even when it has fewer
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line both groups up one-to-one and count; show the shorter-but-denser line actually has more — rebuild the more/fewer comparison
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names the group that fills more table as 'most' when a tighter group actually has more counters

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses track when counting a scattered group, so category totals are wrong
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the count — slide each counter aside as it is counted, or line the group up first; this is a counting lapse, not a sorting error, so steady the count rather than reteach sorting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child double-counts or skips counters in a jumbled pile and gives an unstable total on recount

responseLevels.gap: Sorts inconsistently or leaves objects out, miscounts groups, and picks 'most' by appearance; cannot reliably answer most/fewest
responseLevels.full: Independently sorts every object by one consistent attribute, counts each group accurately, names most/fewest from the counts, and can re-sort the set a different way
responseLevels.partial: Sorts by one attribute and counts with some support, but judges most by space or needs prompting to order the groups

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a mixed pile of coloured counters. Sort them so we can see how many of each colour there are, then tell me which colour we have the most of and which the fewest. (Set the task, then WATCH — do not tell them how to sort.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the DOING is the assessment. A child who has the idea keeps one consistent rule, sorts exhaustively, counts with cardinality, and reads most/fewest from counts; a child who doesn't drifts between attributes, miscounts, or judges 'most' by how much space a group fills. You cannot see this by asking them to describe sorting — you must set the task and observe.
